questions.question: What are the core components of a Kubernetes control plane?
questions.answer: API Server (entry point), etcd (state store), Scheduler (pod placement), Controller Manager (reconciliation loops). Each is stateless except etcd. API Server is the only component that talks to etcd.

questions.question: What is the role of kubelet and kube-proxy on a worker node?
questions.answer: kubelet: registers node, watches PodSpecs via API Server, ensures containers run. kube-proxy: manages iptables/IPVS rules for Service routing. Neither runs in a pod — they're system processes.

questions.question: How does the Kubernetes API Server handle requests?
questions.answer: Authentication → Authorization (RBAC) → Admission Controllers → Validation → etcd write. Mutating admission webhooks run before validating ones. Any step can reject the request.

questions.question: What is etcd and why is it critical?
questions.answer: Distributed key-value store — the single source of truth for all cluster state. Loss of etcd = loss of cluster. Should run as 3 or 5 node cluster for HA. Backup via the following command.
bestPractices: Should run as a 3 or 5 node cluster for High Availability (HA).
Regularly run etcdctl backups.
warnings: Loss of etcd equals loss of the cluster.

questions.question: Explain the Kubernetes reconciliation loop.
questions.answer: Controllers watch desired state (spec) vs actual state (status) and act to close the gap. This is the core pattern — declarative, not imperative. Every controller runs this loop continuously.

questions.question: What happens when you run kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml?
questions.answer: kubectl serialises manifest → sends to API Server → AuthN/AuthZ → admission → stored in etcd → Deployment controller detects new spec → creates ReplicaSet → RS controller creates Pods → Scheduler assigns nodes → kubelet pulls images and starts containers.

questions.question: Difference between kubectl apply vs kubectl create vs kubectl replace?
questions.answer: First command: imperative, fails if exists. Second command: declarative, merges with existing, tracks last-applied annotation. Third command: destructive replace, deletes and recreates. Use the second command for GitOps always.
bestPractices: Use kubectl apply for GitOps always.

questions.question: What is a Namespace and when would you NOT use one?
questions.answer: Virtual cluster for resource isolation and RBAC scoping. Not for strong security isolation — use separate clusters for that. Cluster-scoped resources (Nodes, PVs, ClusterRoles) are not namespaced.
warnings: Namespaces are not for strong security isolation; use separate clusters for that.

questions.question: How does the Kubernetes Scheduler decide where to place a pod?
questions.answer: Filtering: removes nodes that don't meet requirements (resources, taints, affinity). Scoring: ranks remaining nodes. Highest score wins. Tie-breaking is random. Custom schedulers or extenders possible.

questions.question: What is a Custom Resource Definition (CRD)?
questions.answer: Extends the Kubernetes API with custom types. CRD defines the schema; a controller (operator) implements the behaviour. ArgoCD, cert-manager, Crossplane all use CRDs heavily.

questions.question: What is a Pod and why is it the smallest deployable unit?
questions.answer: One or more containers sharing network namespace (same IP) and storage. Co-located by design — sidecar pattern. You never create pods directly in production — use controllers.
warnings: You never create pods directly in production; use controllers.

questions.question: Explain Deployment rolling update strategy.
questions.answer: maxSurge: extra pods during update. maxUnavailable: pods that can be down. Default both 25%. Old RS scaled down, new RS scaled up incrementally. Rollback using the following command.

questions.question: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet vs Job — when to use each?
questions.answer: Deployment: stateless, interchangeable pods. StatefulSet: stable identity, ordered ops, persistent storage per pod. DaemonSet: one pod per node (log agents, monitoring). Job: run-to-completion tasks.

questions.question: What makes StatefulSets different from Deployments?
questions.answer: Stable pod names (web-0, web-1). Stable DNS via headless service. Ordered deploy/scale/delete. PVC per pod that survives pod deletion. Critical for databases, Kafka, Zookeeper.

questions.question: What is an Init Container and when do you use it?
questions.answer: Runs sequentially before app containers. Exits before app starts. Use for: DB migration checks, config generation, waiting for dependencies. Share volumes but not lifecycle with app containers.

questions.question: Explain Pod lifecycle phases.
questions.answer: Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed. Pending: scheduled, image pulling. Running: at least one container running. Succeeded: all containers exited 0. Failed: at least one container exited non-zero. Unknown: node lost.

questions.question: What is a sidecar container pattern?
questions.answer: Helper container in same pod sharing network and volumes. Examples: log shipper (Promtail), service mesh proxy (Envoy), secret rotation agent. Tight coupling is intentional.

questions.question: How do resource requests and limits work?
questions.answer: Request: guaranteed allocation, used for scheduling decisions. Limit: hard cap. CPU is throttled at limit. Memory OOMKilled at limit. Always set both — no limits = noisy neighbour risk.
bestPractices: Always set both resource requests and limits.
warnings: Not setting limits exposes you to noisy neighbour risks.

questions.question: What happens when a pod is OOMKilled?
questions.answer: Container exceeds memory limit → kernel OOM killer terminates it → kubelet restarts it per restartPolicy. Check using the following command and see OOMKilled in last state. Fix: increase limit or fix memory leak.

questions.question: What are liveness, readiness, and startup probes?
questions.answer: Liveness: is container alive? Fail → restart. Readiness: is container ready for traffic? Fail → remove from Service endpoints. Startup: gives slow-starting containers time before liveness kicks in. Don't make liveness too aggressive.
warnings: Don't make liveness probes too aggressive as they can cause restart loops for slow starters.

questions.question: Explain Pod Disruption Budgets (PDB).
questions.answer: Limits voluntary disruptions (drain, upgrades). minAvailable or maxUnavailable. Protects against all pods evicting simultaneously. Required for production HA — without PDB a node drain can take down your service.
bestPractices: PDB is required for production High Availability (HA) to prevent node drains from taking down services.

questions.question: What is a ReplicaSet and do you ever create one directly?
questions.answer: Ensures N pod replicas running. Deployment manages RS — never create RS directly. Deployment adds rollout/rollback on top of RS. RS selector is immutable — label changes require new RS.
warnings: Never create ReplicaSets directly; let Deployments manage them.

questions.question: Explain Kubernetes networking model.
questions.answer: Every pod gets unique IP. Pods can communicate without NAT. Nodes can communicate with pods without NAT. No IP masquerading by default. Implemented by CNI plugins (Calico, Cilium, Flannel).

questions.question: What is a Service and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Stable DNS and VIP for a set of pods. Pods are ephemeral with changing IPs — Service provides stable endpoint. Uses label selectors to find backend pods. kube-proxy maintains iptables/IPVS rules.

questions.question: ClusterIP vs NodePort vs LoadBalancer vs ExternalName?
questions.answer: ClusterIP: internal only. NodePort: exposes on every node's IP:port (30000-32767). LoadBalancer: provisions cloud LB. ExternalName: CNAME to external DNS. Use ClusterIP + Ingress in production, not NodePort.
bestPractices: Use ClusterIP + Ingress in production, rather than NodePort.

questions.question: What is a headless Service?
questions.answer: Setting the first option disables the virtual IP (VIP). No VIP created. DNS returns pod IPs directly. Required for StatefulSets — enables stable DNS per pod (web-0.svc.ns.svc.cluster.local). Also used for service discovery without load balancing.

questions.question: How does Ingress work?
questions.answer: API object defining routing rules. Ingress Controller (NGINX, ALB) watches Ingress objects and configures itself. Rules: host-based or path-based routing to Services. Requires controller — Ingress object alone does nothing.
warnings: An Ingress object alone does nothing; it requires an Ingress Controller to be running.

questions.question: What is a NetworkPolicy and what is the default behaviour without one?
questions.answer: Default: all pods can communicate with all pods (allow all). NetworkPolicy adds whitelist rules for ingress/egress. Requires CNI that supports it (Calico, Cilium — NOT Flannel). Once any policy selects a pod, deny-all applies for unmatched traffic.
warnings: Once any policy selects a pod, deny-all applies for unmatched traffic.

questions.question: Explain CoreDNS in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: Cluster DNS server. Resolves service.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Each pod gets the first configuration file pointing to CoreDNS ClusterIP. Search domains allow short names. Customisable via ConfigMap for stubzones, rewrites.

questions.question: What is kube-proxy and how does it implement Services?
questions.answer: Runs on each node. Watches Service/Endpoint objects. Programs iptables (default) or IPVS rules. iptables: random pod selection per connection. IPVS: more efficient, multiple algorithms. Pure userspace mode is legacy.

questions.question: How does DNS resolution work for a pod calling another service?
questions.answer: App calls 'myservice'. Search path in the first file tries: myservice.namespace.svc.cluster.local → myservice.svc.cluster.local → myservice.cluster.local. CoreDNS resolves to ClusterIP. kube-proxy routes to pod IP.

questions.question: What is a CNI plugin and name three?
questions.answer: Container Network Interface — standard for pod networking. Calico: BGP-based, supports NetworkPolicy, widely used. Cilium: eBPF-based, L7 policy, observability. Flannel: simple overlay, no NetworkPolicy. AWS VPC CNI: native VPC IPs for EKS.

questions.question: How does pod-to-pod communication work across nodes?
questions.answer: Depends on CNI. Flannel: VXLAN overlay encapsulates packets. Calico: BGP routes pod CIDRs between nodes — no encapsulation overhead. AWS VPC CNI: pods get VPC IPs, native routing via VPC route tables.

questions.question: What is an Endpoint and EndpointSlice?
questions.answer: Endpoint: maps Service to pod IPs:ports. Auto-created/updated by endpoint controller. EndpointSlice: shards endpoints into 100-pod chunks — solves etcd and kube-proxy scalability at large scale. EPS is default since 1.21.

questions.question: How do you expose a gRPC service in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: gRPC uses HTTP/2. NGINX Ingress needs the first and second configurations or the third backend. ALB Ingress: set the fourth and fifth options. Service must use port name 'grpc' or 'h2c'. TLS passthrough avoids termination issues.
bestPractices: Use TLS passthrough to avoid termination issues for gRPC.

questions.question: Explain PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, and StorageClass.
questions.answer: PV: actual storage resource (EBS, NFS). PVC: request for storage by a pod. StorageClass: defines provisioner and parameters for dynamic provisioning. PVC binds to PV by size/accessMode/storageClass. Dynamic: SC creates PV automatically.

questions.question: What are the access modes for PersistentVolumes?
questions.answer: RWO (ReadWriteOnce): one node at a time. ROX (ReadOnlyMany): many nodes, read only. RWX (ReadWriteMany): many nodes, read/write — NFS, EFS. RWOP (ReadWriteOncePod): single pod only, since 1.22. EBS only supports RWO.

questions.question: What is the reclaim policy on a PersistentVolume?
questions.answer: Retain: PV not deleted when PVC released — manual cleanup. Delete: PV and backing storage deleted with PVC (default for dynamic). Recycle: deprecated. Always use Retain for production databases.
bestPractices: Always use Retain reclaim policy for production databases.

questions.question: How does a StatefulSet handle PVC lifecycle?
questions.answer: Each pod gets its own PVC via the first setting. PVC survives pod deletion — reattaches to replacement pod with same ordinal. Deleting StatefulSet does NOT delete PVCs. Must delete PVCs manually.
warnings: Deleting a StatefulSet does NOT delete its PVCs; they must be cleaned up manually.

questions.question: What is a StorageClass and how does dynamic provisioning work?
questions.answer: SC defines provisioner (like the first one), parameters (like the second one), and reclaimPolicy. PVC references SC → provisioner creates backing storage → PV created and bound automatically. No pre-provisioning needed.

questions.question: What is a CSI driver?
questions.answer: Container Storage Interface — standard for storage plugins. Replaced in-tree volume plugins. AWS EBS CSI, EFS CSI, GCP PD CSI. Enables out-of-tree development — storage vendors ship their own CSI drivers.

questions.question: ConfigMap vs Secret — differences and when to use each?
questions.answer: ConfigMap: non-sensitive config (env vars, config files). Secret: sensitive data, base64 encoded (NOT encrypted by default). Both mountable as volumes or env vars. Encrypt Secrets at rest via KMS — base64 is not security.
bestPractices: Encrypt Secrets at rest via KMS.
warnings: Secrets are only base64 encoded, which is not encryption. They are not secure by default.

questions.question: How do you mount a Secret as a file vs environment variable?
questions.answer: Volume mount: secret appears as files in pod — updates propagate automatically (with delay). EnvVar: set at container start — does NOT update on secret rotation. Prefer volume mounts for credentials that rotate.
bestPractices: Prefer volume mounts for credentials that rotate to allow automatic updates without container restarts.

questions.question: Explain Kubernetes RBAC components.
questions.answer: Role/ClusterRole: defines verbs (get, list, watch, create, delete) on resources. RoleBinding: namespace-scoped binding to subject. ClusterRoleBinding: cluster-wide. Subjects: User, Group, ServiceAccount. Principle of least privilege always.
bestPractices: Always follow the principle of least privilege in RBAC configuration.

questions.question: What is a ServiceAccount and why does a pod need one?
questions.answer: Identity for pod processes to authenticate to API Server. Every pod gets default SA unless specified. Token auto-mounted at the following path. Disable auto-mount for pods that don't need API access.
bestPractices: Disable auto-mounting of ServiceAccount tokens for pods that do not need to query the Kubernetes API.

questions.question: How does IRSA work on EKS?
questions.answer: EKS has OIDC provider. SA annotated with IAM role ARN. Pod gets OIDC JWT via projected volume. AWS SDK calls STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with JWT. STS validates against EKS OIDC provider. Returns temp creds. No node-level IAM needed.

questions.question: What are Admission Controllers?
questions.answer: Plugins that intercept API requests after AuthZ. Mutating: can modify objects (inject sidecars, add labels). Validating: can reject objects. Order: mutating runs first. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno use validating webhooks. Critical for policy enforcement.

questions.question: What replaced PodSecurityPolicy?
questions.answer: Pod Security Admission (PSA) since 1.25. Three levels: privileged (anything), baseline (minimal restrictions), restricted (hardened). Applied via namespace labels. OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for custom policies beyond PSA.

questions.question: How do you prevent privilege escalation in a pod?
questions.answer: Use the first parameter with the following settings. Combine with restricted PSA and NetworkPolicy for defence in depth.
bestPractices: Combine securityContext settings with restricted PSA and NetworkPolicies for defense-in-depth.

questions.question: What is a Kubernetes audit log?
questions.answer: Records who did what to which resource and when. Stored at API Server level. Policies define what to log (metadata/request/response body). Essential for compliance and incident investigation. Ship to SIEM — CloudWatch Logs on EKS.
bestPractices: Ship audit logs to a SIEM (such as CloudWatch Logs on EKS) for compliance and incident investigation.

questions.question: How do you rotate a Secret in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Update Secret value → pods using volume mounts get update within kubelet sync period (~1 min). Pods using env vars do NOT get update — must restart. For certificates: cert-manager auto-rotates 30 days before expiry and triggers pod rollout.
warnings: Pods using Secret environment variables will NOT automatically pick up Secret updates; they must be restarted.

questions.question: What is Falco and what does it do?
questions.answer: Runtime security tool. Watches kernel syscalls via eBPF/kernel module. Detects anomalous behaviour: shell in container, unexpected outbound connection, privilege escalation. Alerts to stdout/Slack/SIEM. CNCF project.

questions.question: How does network segmentation work with NetworkPolicy?
questions.answer: Default deny all ingress: the first setting with no ingress rules. Then whitelist explicitly. Namespace selector limits cross-namespace traffic. Egress policies control outbound. Test with the second command and the third command before going live.
bestPractices: Implement default deny all ingress by default, then explicitly whitelist traffic.
Test policies using kubectl exec + curl before applying in production.

questions.question: How does Prometheus scrape metrics from Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Prometheus polls the first endpoint at scrape_interval (default 15s). ServiceMonitor CRDs (kube-prometheus-stack) auto-discover targets by label. Pod annotations (the second configuration) for simple discovery. Metrics in exposition format.

questions.question: What is a recording rule in Prometheus and why use it?
questions.answer: Pre-computes expensive PromQL and stores as new metric. Reduces query time for dashboards. Example: record job:request_rate:5m from the following calculation. Run expensive aggregations once, query result cheaply.

questions.question: How do you alert on pod restarts in Prometheus?
questions.answer: Alert query: the first expression. Group by pod and namespace. Add severity label. Annotate with runbook URL. Route to correct receiver via Alertmanager. Test with the second command.

questions.question: What is Loki and how does it differ from Elasticsearch?
questions.answer: Loki indexes only labels — not full text. Low storage cost. Fast label queries. Designed for Kubernetes log streams. ELK indexes everything — powerful full-text search but expensive at scale. Loki integrates natively with Grafana.

questions.question: How does distributed tracing work in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: App instrumented with OpenTelemetry SDK. Each request gets trace ID + span ID in headers (W3C TraceContext). Each service creates child span, passes headers downstream. Spans shipped to collector (Jaeger/Tempo). Visualise full request path across services.

questions.question: What are the four golden signals of SRE?
questions.answer: Latency: how long requests take. Traffic: requests per second. Errors: failed request rate. Saturation: resource utilisation (CPU, memory, queue depth). Monitor these for every service. Use p99 not average for latency.
bestPractices: Use p99 latency instead of average latency to represent actual user experiences accurately.

questions.question: How do you correlate logs, metrics, and traces in Grafana?
questions.answer: Exemplars: embed trace IDs in Prometheus metrics. Click metric spike → jump to trace. Derived fields in Loki: regex extract trace ID from log line → link to Jaeger. Grafana datasource links connect the three pillars.

questions.question: What is a Grafana dashboard variable and why use it?
questions.answer: Template variable populated from datasource query (e.g. the following query). Makes dashboard reusable across namespaces/clusters. Chained variables (cluster → namespace → pod). Reduces dashboard sprawl.

questions.question: How do you size Prometheus storage?
questions.answer: Estimate: ingestion_rate × bytes_per_sample × retention_days. Default 2 bytes/sample compressed. 1M series × 15s scrape × 30d ≈ ~200GB. Use the first setting to Thanos/Cortex/Mimir for long-term storage and HA.
bestPractices: Use remote_write to offload long-term storage and high-availability needs to external systems like Thanos/Cortex/Mimir.

questions.question: What are taints and tolerations?
questions.answer: Taint on node: repels pods that don't tolerate it. Formatted as the first snippet. Effects: the second option (won't schedule), the third option (soft), the fourth option (evict existing). Toleration on pod: allows scheduling on tainted node. Used for dedicated nodes (GPU, spot).

questions.question: What is node affinity vs pod affinity vs taints?
questions.answer: Node affinity: attract pod to nodes with specific labels (requiredDuringScheduling = hard, preferred = soft). Pod affinity: co-locate with pods matching selector. Pod anti-affinity: spread pods across nodes/zones for HA. Taints: node-side repulsion.

questions.question: How does HPA work and what metrics can it use?
questions.answer: Watches metrics via metrics-server (CPU/memory) or custom/external metrics API. Calculates: ceil(current_replicas × current_metric/target). Updates Deployment replicas. Cooldown prevents thrashing. Custom metrics: Prometheus Adapter bridges PromQL to HPA.

questions.question: What is VPA and when does it conflict with HPA?
questions.answer: VPA adjusts CPU/memory requests/limits based on historical usage. Recreate mode restarts pods to apply. Don't use VPA and HPA on CPU/memory simultaneously — they fight. Use HPA on custom metrics + VPA for resource right-sizing.
bestPractices: Combine HPA on custom business/traffic metrics with VPA for resource right-sizing.
warnings: Don't use VPA and HPA on CPU/memory resource metrics simultaneously as they conflict and 'fight' each other.

questions.question: What is Cluster Autoscaler?
questions.answer: Scales node groups based on unschedulable pods (scale up) and underutilised nodes (scale down). Talks to cloud provider API. On EKS: integrates with ASG. Karpenter is next-gen alternative — provisions nodes directly, faster and more flexible.

questions.question: What is a LimitRange and ResourceQuota?
questions.answer: LimitRange: sets default requests/limits and min/max per container in a namespace. ResourceQuota: caps total resources (CPU, memory, PVC count, pod count) per namespace. Together enforce multi-tenant resource governance.
bestPractices: Enforce LimitRanges and ResourceQuotas in multi-tenant environments to restrict resource hogging.

questions.question: What are QoS classes in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Guaranteed: requests = limits for all containers. Burstable: requests set but != limits. BestEffort: no requests or limits. OOM kill order: BestEffort first, then Burstable, Guaranteed last. Set Guaranteed for critical production pods.
bestPractices: Set QoS class to Guaranteed for critical production workloads to minimize OOM kill risks.

questions.question: What is Karpenter and how does it differ from Cluster Autoscaler?
questions.answer: Karpenter provisions individual nodes directly via EC2 API — not ASG. The first and second resources define constraints. Faster provisioning (seconds vs minutes). Bin-packing aware. Consolidation: replaces underutilised nodes. AWS-native, replacing CA on EKS.

questions.question: What is GitOps and what are its four principles?
questions.answer: Git as single source of truth. Desired state declared in Git. Approved changes via Git (PR/merge). Software agents enforce and alert on drift. Weaveworks coined the term. ArgoCD and Flux are the main implementations.

questions.question: How does ArgoCD sync work?
questions.answer: ArgoCD compares live cluster state against Git manifest every 3 min (default). Diff = OutOfSync. Sync applies manifests via the first command. Self-heal: auto-sync OutOfSync apps. Hard refresh bypasses cache. App-of-Apps: one root app manages child apps.

questions.question: What is an ArgoCD ApplicationSet?
questions.answer: Generates multiple Application objects from one template. Generators: cluster (per registered cluster), git directory (per folder), list, matrix (combination). Drives multi-cluster/multi-env deployments from single manifest. No manual app creation per cluster.

questions.question: How do you handle secrets in GitOps?
questions.answer: Never store plaintext secrets in Git. Options: Sealed Secrets (encrypt in repo, decrypt in cluster), External Secrets Operator (pull from AWS Secrets Manager/Vault), SOPS (git-crypt alternative). ESO + AWS Secrets Manager is current best practice.
bestPractices: Use External Secrets Operator (ESO) integrated with AWS Secrets Manager or Vault as a best practice.
warnings: Never store plaintext secrets in Git repositories.

questions.question: What is Helm and how does ArgoCD use it?
questions.answer: Helm: Kubernetes package manager. Chart: templates + values. ArgoCD supports Helm natively — renders chart server-side, stores rendered manifests. ArgoCD tracks chart version + values in Git. Avoid running the first command directly — let ArgoCD manage lifecycle.
warnings: Avoid running helm install directly when using ArgoCD; let ArgoCD manage the chart lifecycle.

questions.question: Difference between Kustomize and Helm?
questions.answer: Kustomize: overlay-based, no templating language, pure YAML patching. Base + overlays for env differences. Helm: Go templates, values files, packaging and distribution focus. Kustomize built into the first command. Use Kustomize for simple env differences, Helm for distributable packages.

questions.question: How do you do a canary deployment with ArgoCD?
questions.answer: Argo Rollouts: custom Rollout resource replaces Deployment. Canary steps: the first four instructions. Integrates with Ingress/service mesh for traffic splitting. Analysis templates run metrics checks before promotion. Automatic rollback on failure.

questions.question: What is ArgoCD drift detection and self-healing?
questions.answer: Controller continuously compares live state vs Git. Any out-of-band change (manual execution of the first command) creates drift. Self-heal: ArgoCD reverts drift automatically. Can disable self-heal for specific resources with the second annotation.

questions.question: How do you manage multi-cluster with ArgoCD?
questions.answer: Hub-spoke: single ArgoCD in control-plane cluster. Spoke clusters registered via the first command (stores kubeconfig secret). ApplicationSets deploy to all clusters via cluster generator. Each spoke needs ArgoCD's SA to have appropriate RBAC.

questions.question: A pod is stuck in Pending — how do you debug?
questions.answer: Run the first command and check Events. Common: Insufficient cpu/memory (increase requests or add nodes), no matching node (check taints/affinity), PVC not bound (check StorageClass/PV), image pull backoff (check imagePullSecrets).

questions.question: A pod is CrashLoopBackOff — your approach?
questions.answer: Run the first command (to see crashed container logs) and the second command (to check exit code — 137=OOMKill, 1=app error, 126/127=command not found). Check liveness probe — may be killing healthy container. Check resource limits.

questions.question: Service is not routing traffic to pods — how do you debug?
questions.answer: Run the first command — if empty, label selector mismatch. Run the second command to check selector vs pod labels. Run the third command. Check NetworkPolicy. Check readiness probe — pod may be Running but not Ready.

questions.question: Node is NotReady — what do you check?
questions.answer: Run the first command to check Conditions and Events. SSH to node and run the second command. Check disk pressure (the third command), memory pressure (the fourth command), PID pressure. Check CNI plugin running. Run the fifth command for logs.

questions.question: How do you debug networking issues between pods?
questions.answer: First run the first command (direct). Then run the second command. Then run the third command. Narrows to: pod IP routing, service DNS, kube-proxy. Use the fourth command with netshoot image for network tools. Check NetworkPolicy.

questions.question: kubectl get pods shows pod running but app returns 502 — why?
questions.answer: Pod running but readiness probe failing → not in endpoints. Or pod restarting (CrashLoopBackOff coming). Or app listening on wrong port. Check by running the second, third, and fourth commands for probe failures.

questions.question: How do you investigate high memory usage in a cluster?
questions.answer: Run the first command (node level). Run the second command (pod level). Run the third command for allocated vs actual. Check OOMKilled events. Look for memory leaks in app (compare RSS over time in Grafana). Check JVM heap if Java app.

questions.question: ArgoCD shows OutOfSync but you didn't change anything — why?
questions.answer: Server-side field injection (admission webhooks, defaulting). Resource was modified out-of-band. Timestamp/generation fields differ. Fix: use server-side apply, add the first option in ArgoCD app spec for fields you can't control.

questions.question: How do you do a zero-downtime deployment?
questions.answer: Set the first parameter. Ensure readiness probe is accurate. Set the second and third parameters (or use Argo Rollouts canary). Ensure PodDisruptionBudget. Use the fourth hook with sleep to drain connections before pod terminates. Set the fifth parameter.
bestPractices: Set maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 for zero-downtime rolling updates.
Use preStop hooks with sleep to drain active network connections before termination.

questions.question: A node is running out of disk — what's your immediate response?
questions.answer: Run the first command (stop new scheduling). Run the second command — check disk pressure taint. SSH to node and run the third and fourth commands. Clean dangling images with the fifth command. Check the sixth path for log growth. Consider node drain if severe.

questions.question: How do you force delete a pod stuck in Terminating?
questions.answer: Run the following command. This removes from etcd immediately — kubelet may still clean up. Use only when node is unreachable or pod is truly stuck. Understand why it got stuck first (finalizers, volume unmount).
warnings: Force deleting a pod bypasses graceful termination and removes it from etcd immediately. Use only when the node is unreachable or the pod is truly stuck.

questions.question: Design a zero-downtime deployment pipeline for a microservice.
questions.answer: GitHub Actions: test → build → Trivy scan → push ECR. ArgoCD watches Git. Rollout strategy: maxUnavailable 0, maxSurge 1. Readiness probe gates traffic. PDB ensures minimum availability. Argo Rollouts for canary. Automated rollback on error rate SLO breach.
bestPractices: Automate rollbacks based on error rate SLO breaches.

questions.question: How would you implement multi-tenancy in a single cluster?
questions.answer: Namespace per tenant. ResourceQuota + LimitRange per namespace. NetworkPolicy default-deny with explicit allow. RBAC: tenant SA can only access own namespace. OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement. Separate node pools for noisy-neighbour isolation if needed.
bestPractices: Enforce network segmentation using a default-deny NetworkPolicy.
Isolate workloads physically using dedicated node pools for noisy neighbors if needed.

questions.question: Your cluster is under heavy load — how do you scale?
questions.answer: Immediate: the first command or HPA will handle pods. Check node capacity: if saturated, Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter adds nodes. Medium-term: review resource requests (VPA). Long-term: shard workloads across clusters. Enable KEDA for event-driven scaling.

questions.question: How would you migrate a stateful application to Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Assess: storage requirements, backup strategy, failure modes. Use StatefulSet with PVC per pod. Run database outside cluster or use operator (RDS, CloudNative PG). Migration: blue/green with DNS cutover. Never lift-shift a DB without operator or managed service.
warnings: Never lift-and-shift a database directly to Kubernetes without using a database operator or managed service.

questions.question: How do you implement disaster recovery for a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.answer: Multi-region clusters with ArgoCD ApplicationSets. Velero for PV backup to S3. etcd snapshots on schedule. GitOps: cluster state reconstructable from Git in minutes. RTO/RPO defined per service. Test DR quarterly with actual failover.
bestPractices: Test disaster recovery plans quarterly with actual workload failover.
Configure cluster state to be completely reconstructable from Git repositories (GitOps).

questions.question: A security team says a container is making unexpected outbound calls — how do you respond?
questions.answer: Immediate: NetworkPolicy egress deny-all for the namespace. Investigate: the first command with the second or third command in pod. Check Falco alerts for syscall anomalies. Review image with Trivy for malware. Check if env vars expose secrets that may be exfiltrated. Postmortem after containment.
bestPractices: Enforce default-deny NetworkPolicies to restrict outbound traffic immediately when malicious behavior is suspected.
Conduct postmortems after containment.

questions.question: How do you reduce costs in a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.answer: Right-size requests with VPA recommendations. Cluster Autoscaler scale-down aggressive settings. Spot/preemptible instances for stateless workloads. Delete unused namespaces and PVCs. Karpenter consolidation. Set resource quotas to prevent waste. Review unused load balancers.
bestPractices: Use VPA recommendations to right-size requests.
Utilize spot/preemptible instances for stateless, resilient workloads.
Delete unused namespaces and PVCs to reduce waste.

questions.question: How would you onboard a new team to your Kubernetes platform?
questions.answer: Self-service namespace via GitOps PR. RBAC template via ClusterRole binding. Resource quota defaults. Onboarding doc: how to deploy, how to read logs, how to debug. Golden path Helm chart or Kustomize base. Internal developer portal (Backstage) for self-service.

questions.question: Explain how you would implement secret rotation with zero downtime.
questions.answer: Secrets manager stores secret. External Secrets Operator syncs to K8s Secret on schedule. App reads from volume mount (not env var). New secret version deployed → ESO updates K8s Secret → kubelet propagates to volume → app reloads config without restart. Test rotation in staging first.
bestPractices: Test secret rotation flows in staging first before applying to production.
Ensure the application reloads configurations automatically from volume mounts without needing restarts.

questions.question: If you had to rebuild this cluster from scratch tomorrow, what would you do differently?
questions.answer: Cluster API or Terraform for cluster IaC from day 1. External Secrets from day 1 — not Sealed Secrets. OPA Gatekeeper policies before first workload. Structured logging standard across all apps. SLO dashboards before features. GitOps for everything including cluster bootstrap (ArgoCD App-of-Apps).
bestPractices: Adopt Terraform/Cluster API for cluster IaC and GitOps bootstrap from day one.
Implement OPA Gatekeeper policies and structured logging prior to deploying any business workloads.
